steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Crowdsourcing platforms let dataset developers distribute data labelling microtasks in a way that is efficient and scalable, so they are a natural choice when developers want to get dataset annotations cheaply and efficiently. This short survey paper looks at the challenges and decision points that come from crowdsourced dataset annotation. Our question is: who is annotating the data, and why is that important? We look at how the ethical concerns of data annotation intersect with who the annotators are, with the social structures around their work, and with how their individual perspectives can get encoded in the dataset labels. The data from crowdwork tasks is shaped by a range of social factors, and the datasets workers help build keep shaping systems long after the workers stop being involved. We argue that this impacts future models built from this data, and that understanding the perspectives captured in datasets is crucial for understanding the resulting models and their potential social impact.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Crowdsourcing platforms let dataset developers distribute data labelling microtasks in a way that is efficient and scalable, so they are a natural choice when developers want to get dataset annotations cheaply and efficiently. This short survey paper looks at the challenges and decision points that come from crowdsourced dataset annotation. Our question is: who is annotating the data, and why is that important? We look at how the ethical concerns of data annotation intersect with who the annotators are, with the social structures around their work, and with how their individual perspectives can get encoded in the dataset labels. The data from crowdwork tasks is shaped by a range of social factors, and the datasets workers help build keep shaping systems long after the workers stop being involved. We argue that this impacts future models built from this data, and that understanding the perspectives captured in datasets is crucial for understanding the resulting models and their potential social impact.

Our work complements and extends prior scholarship that has looked at ethical considerations in crowdsourcing. It is different from that scholarship because we focus on unresolved ethical problems in crowdsourcing that are specifically about individual worker subjectivity and individual worker experiences. First we outline a comprehensive set of concerns about how annotators' individual and collective social experiences, and also their working conditions, may impact the nature of the data they provide for machine learning development, in particular the biases that may be captured in those datasets and propagated through them. Then, based on this analysis, we give a set of ethical considerations and recommendations for dataset developers. These apply to different steps of a typical data annotation pipeline, from task formulation to dataset release.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
By enabling efficient and scalable distribution of data labelling microtasks, crowdsourcing platforms are a natural choice for dataset developers who want to generate dataset annotations cheaply and efficiently. In this short survey paper we explore the inherent challenges and decision points that stem from crowdsourced dataset annotation. In particular, we ask: who is annotating the data, and why is that important? We consider how the ethical concerns of data annotation intersect with the identities of the annotators, the social structures surrounding their work, and how their individual perspectives may become encoded in the dataset labels. Data generated in crowdwork tasks is shaped by a range of social factors, and the datasets that workers help to build continue to shape systems long after worker engagement ends. We argue that this impacts future models built from this data, and that understanding the perspectives captured within datasets is crucial to understanding the resulting models and their potential social impact.

Our work complements and extends prior scholarship examining ethical considerations related to crowdsourcing [1,2,3,4]. It is distinct from this scholarship in that we focus on unresolved ethical problems in crowdsourcing that relate specifically to individual worker subjectivity and individual worker experiences. We start by outlining a comprehensive set of concerns about how annotators' individual and collective social experiences, as well as their working conditions, may impact the nature of the data they provide for machine learning development, in particular the biases that may be captured in and propagated through those datasets. Based on this analysis, we then offer a set of ethical considerations and recommendations for dataset developers that apply to different steps of a typical data annotation pipeline, from task formulation to dataset release.

References:
[1] Vakharia and Lease (2015) Donna Vakharia and Matthew Lease. 2015. Beyond Mechanical Turk: An analysis of paid crowd work platforms. Proceedings of the iConference (2015), 1–17.
[2] Schlagwein et al . (2019) Daniel Schlagwein, Dubravka Cecez-Kecmanovic, and Benjamin Hanckel. 2019. Ethical norms and issues in crowdsourcing practices: A Habermasian analysis. Information Systems Journal 29, 4 (2019), 811–837. https://doi.org/10.1111/isj.12227 arXiv:https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/isj.12227
[3] Kocsis and de Vreede (2016) David Kocsis and Gert-Jan de Vreede. 2016. Towards a taxonomy of ethical considerations in crowdsourcing. (2016).
[4] Shmueli et al . (2021) Boaz Shmueli, Jan Fell, Soumya Ray, and Lun-Wei Ku. 2021. Beyond Fair Pay: Ethical Implications of NLP Crowdsourcing. arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.10097 (2021).
